transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. [Name]. Welcome in—what brings you here today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thanks for seeing me. So, the thing is, I'm a supervisor for a sales team—mostly B2B stuff, not retail—which means there's a ton of tracking and reporting involved. And honestly, it's just getting to the point where I'm driving myself crazy, and my wife finally told me I needed to talk to somebody. 

What brings me in is that I just keep making these really dumb mistakes on my sales reports. Like, I’ll be looking right at the team dashboard, pulling the weekly metrics, and I’ll somehow copy down the completely wrong numbers into the main spreadsheet. Or we have these specific compliance procedures I have to sign off on for my reps, and I'll just completely miss a line that I was supposed to check. 

And the worst part—the part that really makes me feel like I'm losing my mind—is that I always think I went over it. I swear I do. I’ll sit there, trace my finger down the screen, tell myself everything looks good, and then my manager will email me an hour later asking why the figures are completely off. It’s so embarrassing, you know? I’ve been doing this a while, I worked my way up to supervisor without a college degree, so I feel like I have to prove myself, and I shouldn’t be messing up the basic data entry part of my job. But it just keeps happening no matter how many times I tell myself to slow down and look at the page.
When you go back over your work, do you feel a strong urge or anxiety that drives you to recheck it repeatedly, or do you simply fail to notice the errors even though you looked at the numbers?

No, it’s not really an anxiety thing, you know? Like, I don’t sit there feeling this intense panic or this... this burning need to check it over and over again like I’m obsessed with it. It’s not like that at all. It’s actually the second thing you said. I just completely fail to see it. 

And that’s the part that drives me up a wall! I mean, I’ll be sitting at my desk—I have this dual monitor setup in my home office, right? So I’ve got the CRM open on the left screen, and the master Excel sheet on the right screen. And I will look directly at the left screen, see that one of my guys, let's say Dave, closed twenty-two units. I look back at the right screen, type in twelve, and then when I go back to proofread before I send the final email out to the regional director, I’ll look right at that twelve and my brain just... tells me it’s a twenty-two. 

It’s like my eyes are skimming over the page, but the information just isn't actually connecting in my head. I’m not anxious about the numbers until *after* I get caught making a mistake. Then, sure, I feel terrible and my stomach drops. But in the moment when I'm doing it? I’m just trying to get through the paperwork so I can get back to managing my team, because that’s what I’m actually good at. I’m good with people, I’m good at coaching my reps on closing deals, but this admin stuff... I just look right at the mistake and it registers as completely fine. I'll even highlight the cells sometimes, thinking that'll force me to look closer, and I still just breeze right past the error. It's like I have a blind spot.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a persistent pattern of careless mistakes on detailed clerical/administrative tasks (misreading numbers, missing compliance check-off lines) despite visually looking directly at the correct information—consistent with a core inattentive deficit rather than intentional carelessness. Critically, he explicitly denies the anxious, obsessive quality of checking/rechecking seen in OCD (F42): there is no distressing urge or compulsion to re-verify, and anxiety only emerges after an error is discovered, not during the task. This pattern—chronic difficulty sustaining attention to fine detail, failure to notice obvious discrepancies despite active effort (highlighting cells, tracing with finger), and resulting functional impairment at work—is characteristic of an attention-deficit disturbance (F90.0). No hyperactive/impulsive symptoms were reported, but ICD-10 F90.0 (Disturbance of activity and attention) encompasses inattentive-predominant presentations of ADHD.
